1.pericope_label: The word of the Lord came unto me again, saying, What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge? As I live, saith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel. Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch take the proverb apart grammatically: the verb is an imperfect rather than the perfect used by the other prophet who quotes the saying, so the sense is that fathers eat sour grapes and are accustomed to eat them; the noun for fathers carries no article, because the saying applies to whoever eats them; and the phrase must be rendered in the land of Israel rather than concerning it, an interpreter being named and corrected on the point. Ellicott agrees on the rendering, taking it to mean among the people, both those at Jerusalem and those in captivity, notes that the same proverb is quoted and condemned by another prophet, and reads the declaration that all souls are God's as the basis of the whole teaching, since if all alike belong to him he has no occasion to punish one lest another escape; he also fixes the vocabulary, that soul here means the person rather than the immortal part, and that dying is used broadly for suffering punishment.

Gill treats the naming of the word of the Lord as giving the prophecy weight and authority and marks the section off as a distinct sermon delivered at another time, reads the proverb as spoken concerning the land and of the two tribes rather than the ten, finds the expostulation itself proof that the speakers had no just cause, and observes that God swears by his life because he could swear by no greater. He grounds the claim that all souls are God's in creation, and takes it for property, dominion and accountability. Calvin sees perverse interpreters who purposely twist and tear the teaching of heaven, a world full of men who search the law and the gospel for material to joke with; quotes a Latin poet who told the Romans they must bear the vengeance of the gods for crimes not their own, and asks why that trifler called his own generation undeserving when crimes were rife at Rome; treats the complaint as the testimony of a corrupt nature which throws blame as far from itself as it can; denies that repentance is in view in the oath, since God means only to strike the boasting from under them by making their guilt conspicuous; and refuses the reading that makes all souls are mine a claim of sovereignty on the potter and clay model, holding instead that God shows fatherly love toward the race he formed, as a workman loves his own work.

Clarke states the question the chapter exists to answer, how far the moral evil of a parent extends to his offspring and whether the faults of parents are transferred to children and punished in them, traces the complaint to a misreading of the second commandment and like passages, expects the answer to appear chiefly in another life when every ligament that now binds societies and nations is dissolved and each bears his own burden, and notices that the prophet, having a doctrine to settle which touches the comfort of man and the honour of the divine government, lays aside his usual figure and allegory for the utmost plainness. Wesley glosses the proverb briefly, taking the land for the two tribes, the fathers for forefathers, the eating for sinning, and the children for those unborn who suffer for it, and reads the declaration about souls as showing there can be no colour of partial judgment in God, who is equally God to all.

Henry opens with the maxim that evil manners beget good laws and evil proverbs good prophecies, allows the saying had occasion since God had declared he would visit the iniquity of fathers on children and the prophets had reckoned the sins of earlier kings into the present ruin, the nation being a body politic and a corporation never dying, but holds that what the speakers meant was a reflection on God's equity, showing them unhumbled under the rod, condemning God and justifying themselves; he grants what is true in the figure, that the grapes look well in the temptation and are bitterness itself in the reflection; and he notes that the withdrawal of the proverb is a promise in another prophet and a threatening here, since their own consciences and their neighbours will confirm they had eaten the same sour grapes.

debates.question: Is the proverb spoken concerning the land of Israel or in it?

positions.position: In the land, that is, among the people, both at Jerusalem and in captivity; an interpreter who reads concerning is named and corrected.
Concerning the land, and specifically of the two tribes rather than the ten.

debates.question: What does the declaration that all souls are God's assert?

positions.position: Property, dominion and accountability by right of creation.
Not power but fatherly love toward the race he formed; the potter and clay reading, true in itself, is not what is meant here.
That since all alike are his, he need not punish one lest another escape.
That there can be no colour of partial judgment in one who is equally God to all.

debates.question: What death is threatened against the soul that sins?

positions.position: Spiritual and eternal misery, as distinct from the temporal calamities in which children do sometimes fare the worse for a parent.
Suffering punishment in the broad sense, soul meaning the person rather than the immortal part.
To be manifested particularly in the rewards and punishments of another life.

outliers.claim: Reaches for a Latin poet who told the Romans they must bear the vengeance of the gods for their fathers' crimes until they repaired the temples, and asks why that trifler should call his own generation undeserving when crimes were rife at Rome in his day.

Observes that the prophet drops his usual figure and allegory for this chapter alone, because the doctrine touches the comfort of man and the honour of the divine government and needed the utmost plainness.

themes: The word of the Lord came unto me again, saying,
What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children’s teeth are set on edge?
As I live, saith the Lord God, ye shall not have occasion any more to use this proverb in Israel.
Behold, all souls are mine; as the soul of the father, so also the soul of the son is mine: the soul that sinneth, it shall die.

5.pericope_label: But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right, And hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, neither hath defiled his neighbour’s wife, neither hath come near to a menstruous woman, And hath not oppressed any, but hath restored to the debtor his pledge, hath spoiled none by violence, hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment; He that hath not given forth upon usury, neither hath taken any increase, that hath withdrawn his hand from iniquity, hath executed true judgment between man and man, Hath walked in my statutes, and hath kept my judgments, to deal truly; he is just, he shall surely live, saith the Lord God.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch call the catalogue a picture of the righteousness which has the promise of life and make that righteousness the fulfilling of the law's commandments, religious duties first and then the rest. Ellicott sets out the shape of the passage, general terms at either end with particulars between, and treats the whole as a terse summary of practical duty; he grants that the Lord himself was worshipped in high places against the law but holds the context points to sacrificial idol-feasts, suggests that lifting the eyes covers any longing short of actual worship, notes that borrowing in that society was the resort of the very poor, insists that feeding the hungry and clothing the naked are not left optional in Scripture but positively required and their neglect a sin, and holds that the word rendered usury means not excessive interest but any interest at all, forbidden of a Hebrew and allowed without limit from a foreigner as a law of kindness rather than a regulation of trade.

Gill refuses to read the just man legally, since on those terms no such man exists, and makes the justice evangelical, resting on an imputed righteousness with a principle of grace wrought within, the opening phrase describing the inward frame from which the acts proceed; he notes that eating on a mountain was not unlawful in itself, only that the temples stood there and the sacrifices were eaten in honour of what they served. Calvin describes the method as a general statement followed by chosen species, takes eating for sacrificing by a figure and appeals to the apostle who defines idolatry not by bending the knee to wood or stone but by quoting Moses that the people rose up to play after banqueting, makes the eyes the chief outlet of the affections as a man lifts them to a neighbour's house when he covets it, weighs the phrase tying the idols to the house of Israel as shutting off the plea that they abhorred only heathen gods, restricts the pledge to a garment, a bed or the tools a man earns by, forbids the taking of a millstone since emptying a poor man's workshop is as good as taking his life, calls entering the house to search it robbery, answers the objection that liberality cannot be compelled by saying the bread is yours yet not so yours that you may refuse a hungry brother, and argues at length that interest cannot be condemned without exception since the law is a complete rule of just living and permitted it from strangers, while granting that the trade is illiberal and that no well ordered state tolerates a professed usurer.

Clarke splits the description, holy within and acting by law and equity, and works through the particulars as numbered articles: idolatrous worship performed on hills, where those who sacrificed feasted on the sacrifice and so held communion with the idol; the pledge, which is generally worth more than the debt so that an unprincipled man finds pretences for keeping it; bread and clothing as two branches of one root; and usury, derived from a word meaning to bite because it devours the principal, which he takes for exorbitant profit exacted on need and says bites the receiver in his property and the lender in his salvation. On the promise he reads living upward: the man has lived to God and shall live with him. Wesley glosses briefly, taking the eating for idolatry and the increase for illegal interest, and reads the promise of life as deliverance from famine, pestilence and sword, with good days seen.

debates.question: What kind of righteousness is the just man's?

positions.position: Evangelical, resting on an imputed righteousness with a principle of grace within, since on legal terms no just man exists.
The fulfilling of the law's commandments.
Holy within and acting by law and equity together.

debates.question: Does the prohibition forbid all interest or only oppressive interest?

positions.position: Any interest at all from a Hebrew, the law being one of kindness rather than a rule of trade.
Not all interest; the law is a complete rule of justice and permitted it from strangers, so what matters is the substance rather than the word.
Exorbitant or illegal profit exacted on another's need.

debates.question: What is the life promised to the just man?

positions.position: Deliverance from famine, pestilence and sword, and good days seen.
Life with God: he has lived to God and shall live with him.

outliers.claim: Forbids taking a millstone or a workman's tools in pledge on the ground that emptying a poor man's workshop is as good as taking his life, and calls a creditor's entering the house to search it a species of robbery.
Insists that feeding the hungry and clothing the naked are not optional acts of generosity in Scripture but positively required duties whose neglect is itself sin.

themes: But if a man be just, and do that which is lawful and right,
And hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, neither hath defiled his neighbour’s wife, neither hath come near to a menstruous woman,
And hath not oppressed any, but hath restored to the debtor his pledge, hath spoiled none by violence, hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment;
He that hath not given forth upon usury, neither hath taken any increase, that hath withdrawn his hand from iniquity, hath executed true judgment between man and man,
Hath walked in my statutes, and hath kept my judgments, to deal truly; he is just, he shall surely live, saith the Lord God.

10.pericope_label: If he beget a son that is a robber, a shedder of blood, and that doeth the like to any one of these things, And that doeth not any of those duties, but even hath eaten upon the mountains, and defiled his neighbour’s wife, Hath oppressed the poor and needy, hath spoiled by violence, hath not restored the pledge, and hath lifted up his eyes to the idols, hath committed abomination, Hath given forth upon usury, and hath taken increase: shall he then live? he shall not live: he hath done all these abominations; he shall surely die; his blood shall be upon him. Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father’s sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like, That hath not eaten upon the mountains, neither hath lifted up his eyes to the idols of the house of Israel, hath not defiled his neighbour’s wife, Neither hath oppressed any, hath not withholden the pledge, neither hath spoiled by violence, but hath given his bread to the hungry, and hath covered the naked with a garment, That hath taken off his hand from the poor, that hath not received usury nor increase, hath executed my judgments, hath walked in my statutes; he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live. As for his father, because he cruelly oppressed, spoiled his brother by violence, and did that which is not good among his people, lo, even he shall die in his iniquity.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch head the section with its point in a single line, that the son who avoids his father's sin will live while the father dies for his own, and note that the righteousness of the father does not protect a wicked son from death. Ellicott distinguishes the wording of the two descriptions, the first partitive and the second collective, and denies the inference that whoever commits one sin has committed all; the point is rather that a man who willingly commits any of the forbidden things shows the alienation of his heart and places himself among those who do not intend to abide by the divine will. He observes that the son of a righteous man has advantages and the son of a wicked man hindrances which are not mentioned here, since the object is to set out individual responsibility apart from other issues, that the examples of sin are varied from case to case to show they are only examples, and that the third case was especially suited to refuting the proverb, since here at last was a father who had eaten sour grapes whose son's teeth were not set on edge.

Gill says grace is not conveyed by natural generation though sin is, so that good men often have bad children, and finds an instance in the robber released at the trial, whose name means son of a father and whose own father may for all we know have been a good man; on the third case he names two kings of Judah who were godly sons of idolaters. Calvin lays out the three generations as one design, so that God permits neither the just to lose their promised blessing nor the despisers of his law to escape; he notices that the second catalogue is sharpened, since where the first said only that the man oppressed another this one says the poor and needy, cruelty toward those whose condition should move pity being by so much more atrocious; and he turns the third case directly against the proverb, since if sons really suffered for what their fathers ate, godly men descended from despisers of God would be clear of all their own sins and a good king would have borne the punishment due his idolatrous father. He adds that the quarrel was never about the right but about the fact, nobody having argued that God ought to spare the innocent, the people being so possessed by the error that punishment overruns the guilty that they could not see justice is never robbed of its reward.

Clarke asks the question flatly and answers it, whether the father's holiness shall be imputed to the son, and says it shall not, the man suffering for his own crimes; he has the good grandson laying to heart his father's evil life and what it came to, and closes the account with an even balance, that a man is no more affected by his father's crimes than his father was benefited by his grandfather's righteousness. Wesley notices that the word for blood in the clause laying it upon him is plural and reads two bloods in it, that of the innocent the man murdered and his own, thereby forfeited, so that the whole blame of his misery in time and eternity lies on himself.

Henry treats the wicked son of a godly father as a melancholy but common case and draws the chapter's hardest lesson from it, that grace does not run in the blood nor always attend the means of grace, the race not being to the swift, for then well taught children would do well; God will have us know his grace is his own and his Spirit a free agent, and that though we are tied to give our children a good education he is not tied to bless it, so that here as much as anywhere appear the power of original sin and the necessity of special grace. He allows such a son may prosper a while for his ancestors' piety but insists the descent will not stand him in stead, aggravating both the sin and the condemnation. On the third case he is glad to say that men do not gather grapes of thorns but God sometimes does, taking a branch from a wild olive and grafting it into a good tree, so that where children ordinarily see their parents' sins and do the like, this one sees them and dreads doing the like, refusing to publish his father's shame as the mocking son once did but loathing it and thinking the worse of sin for its being the ruin of his own house.

debates.question: Is one offence enough to condemn, or must the whole catalogue be committed?

positions.position: The first description is partitive and the second collective; committing any one willingly places a man among those who prefer their own will to God's, but this is not because one sin counts as all.
The son who does all these abominations dies for them, his father's holiness not being imputed to him.

debates.question: Why do godly parents so often have wicked children?

positions.position: Because grace does not run in the blood nor always attend the means of grace; God's Spirit is a free agent, and we are tied to educate our children though he is not tied to bless it.
Because grace is not conveyed by natural generation, though sin is.

outliers.claim: Finds an emblem in the robber released at the trial, whose name means son of a father, and remarks that his own father may for all we know have been a good man.
Reads the word for blood in the clause laying it upon the man as a plural, two bloods: that of the innocent he murdered and his own, which he thereby forfeited.

And that doeth not any of those duties, but even hath eaten upon the mountains, and defiled his neighbour’s wife,

That hath taken off his hand from the poor, that hath not received usury nor increase, hath executed my judgments, hath walked in my statutes; he shall not die for the iniquity of his father, he shall surely live.

19.pericope_label: Yet say ye, Why? doth not the son bear the iniquity of the father? When the son hath done that which is lawful and right, and hath kept all my statutes, and hath done them, he shall surely live. The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him. But if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die. All his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him: in his righteousness that he hath done he shall live.

schools.summary: Ellicott would read the people's interruption as a single question rather than two and takes the objection seriously: it seemed to them the law of nature and the teaching of history that a son should bear his father's iniquity, their ideas not having risen to individual responsibility, the individual being still only part of a family or a nation, so they asked why a universal law was reversed. His answer is that no law was reversed, only that a higher law prevailed over a lower, and he observes that the divine word does not argue with the objection but simply repeats itself. On the promise of forgetting he calls the phrase a strong way of expressing the completeness of forgiveness, admits the apparent contradiction that a pardoned man is still seen to suffer through life from what he did, one king's whole reign lying under a cloud after his great sin, and resolves it by saying the natural consequences are not cancelled but run in subservience to a higher moral law, the man's present state deciding whether they will be for his highest gain. He also lays out the architecture of the fourth case, the briefer half being the falling righteous, since the object is to encourage hope in repentance, and the pair stated and then repeated in reverse order for emphasis.

Gill hears blasphemy in the interruption, a quarrel with the prophet and with God over what the speakers claim to feel every day, and takes the repetition of the rule as confirmation. Calvin faces the harder form of the difficulty, that God so often declares he visits the iniquity of fathers upon children to the third and fourth generation, and answers in two moves: first that nobody dies innocent, since the whole race fell in one man so that the curse is partly another's and partly our own, a child being corrupt before birth and the corruption rightly reckoned sin before a sight keener than ours, which is why a psalmist reminded of one sin went back to his conception; and second that the penalty on the children of the impious is chiefly inward, sword and famine and pestilence being visible while the hidden punishment is that God withdraws the spirit of rectitude, gives them up to a reprobate mind and leaves them in the death they were born in. On repentance he warns against the half conversion of those who mingle virtues with vices and think the guilt cancelled if they can produce something creditable, which he likens to serving a master muddy wine mixed with filth as well as dregs, and defines true conversion as beginning when a man renounces himself and completed only when he gives himself to obedience; the forgetting he calls a voluntary oblivion by which the penitent pass at once out of death into life.

Clarke marks the structural turn, that the simple cases are finished and two remain, the wicked man who repents and the righteous man who backslides, and says the transgressions are so completely forgiven that they will not even be mentioned to him, so that if he lives and dies in the recovered state he shall live with God eternally. Wesley resolves the difficulty about the fathers differently: could we see the connexions between persons and between sins, and how easily and undiscerned men come to share the same sins, we should find father and son both guilty and neither punished beyond his own account, Scripture dooming nobody for sins he is wholly free of; the promise as he glosses it is that the son shall not die eternally for his father's iniquity if he does not tread in its steps, nor the father for the son's. He narrows the phrase about not mentioning to exactly its terms, not mentioned to him.

Henry defines what turning requires. Consideration is the first step, since sinners go on precisely because they never consider the end of it; the aversion must then be universal, no reserve kept for one favourite sin, because we do not hate sin as sin unless we hate all of it; and it must be joined to obedience, on God's rule rather than the world's.

debates.question: How can the son not bear the father's iniquity when God declares he visits it to the third and fourth generation?

positions.position: Nobody dies innocent, since all fell in one man; and the punishment visited on such children is chiefly inward, the withdrawal of the Spirit, leaving them in the death they were born in.
Children who suffer do in fact share the sin, though the connexion escapes us; Scripture dooms nobody for sins he is wholly free of.
No law is reversed at all; a higher law simply prevails over a lower, and the divine word does not argue the point but repeats it.

debates.question: If forgiveness is complete, why does the pardoned man still suffer for what he did?

positions.position: The natural consequences are not cancelled but run in subservience to a higher moral law, and the man's present state decides whether they work for his highest gain.
God buries the transgressions by a voluntary oblivion, and the penitent pass at once out of death into life.
They are so completely forgiven that they are not even mentioned to him.

outliers.claim: Likens the half convert who offsets his vices with something creditable to a servant handing his master muddy wine because it has been mixed with filth as well as dregs.
Makes consideration the first step of conversion, on the ground that sinners persist chiefly because they never sit down to consider what the end of their course will be.

themes: Yet say ye, Why? doth not the son bear the iniquity of the father? When the son hath done that which is lawful and right, and hath kept all my statutes, and hath done them, he shall surely live.

The soul that sinneth, it shall die. The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, neither shall the father bear the iniquity of the son: the righteousness of the righteous shall be upon him, and the wickedness of the wicked shall be upon him.
But if the wicked will turn from all his sins that he hath committed, and keep all my statutes, and do that which is lawful and right, he shall surely live, he shall not die.
All his transgressions that he hath committed, they shall not be mentioned unto him: in his righteousness that he hath done he shall live.

23.pericope_label: Have I any pleasure at all that the wicked should die? saith the Lord God: and not that he should return from his ways, and live? But when the righteous turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and doeth according to all the abominations that the wicked man doeth, shall he live? All his righteousness that he hath done shall not be mentioned: in his trespass that he hath trespassed, and in his sin that he hath sinned, in them shall he die. Yet ye say, The way of the Lord is not equal. Hear now, O house of Israel; Is not my way equal? are not your ways unequal? When a righteous man turneth away from his righteousness, and committeth iniquity, and dieth in them; for his iniquity that he hath done shall he die. Again, when the wicked man turneth away from his wickedness that he hath committed, and doeth that which is lawful and right, he shall save his soul alive. Because he considereth, and turneth away from all his transgressions that he hath committed, he shall surely live, he shall not die. Yet saith the house of Israel, The way of the Lord is not equal. O house of Israel, are not my ways equal? are not your ways unequal?

schools.summary: Ellicott makes the question about God's pleasure the fundamental truth underlying both testaments: God created man, ordered both dispensations after the fall and used methods of infinite love to win him back, so his delight can only be in a creature fulfilling the design it was made for; yet neither, as the next verse declares, can he suffer his love to be set at nought and his salvation despised. Where the text speaks of a man saving his own soul alive he qualifies carefully, that this does not mean anyone saves himself by his own power, a question not in view, but that the course of conduct has salvation for its consequence and the choice of it lies with the man. On the complaint about God's way he notes the word means literally weighed out or balanced, so the charge is that God is arbitrary and unjust, while the reply is that he rewards and punishes according to eternal and immutable principles of right, every man reaping what he sowed.

Gill refuses to take the denial of pleasure absolutely, since God does take pleasure in these judgments so far as they fulfil his word, secure the honour of his truth and holiness, glorify his justice and above all reclaim men from their ways; the denial is comparative, mercy being his delight and destruction his strange work. On the falling righteous he denies a truly righteous man can be meant, since nobody is righteous by anything of his own but by the righteousness of Christ, which is God's and can never be lost; the man in view is righteous in his own esteem and his neighbours' account, holding a ceremonial or at best a merely moral righteousness. He also lists how many ways the case had already been put before the complaint was repeated, and calls the repetition stubbornness rather than blindness. Calvin says God desires nothing more earnestly than that those rushing to destruction should turn back, and finds even the heathen, without law or prophets and suffocated by errors, moved by a secret impulse to seek pardon as though the sense that God may be appeased by seekers were born in them; he warns the man who thinks he stands, holds that only perseverance is blessed since a temporary righteousness never profits an apostate, insists the two clauses belong together so that God invites the perishing with open arms while keeping the confident within bounds, and traces the escalation of the complaint, hypocrites finding fault indirectly while pretending not to, accusing God of rigour in the act of excusing themselves, and then, gaining nothing by the double dealing, being inflamed to condemn him outright.

Clarke reads the denial of pleasure absolutely and draws a conclusion from it about decrees: God can do nothing with which he is not pleased and therefore can decree nothing with which he is not pleased, so since he is not pleased with the death of a sinner he cannot have decreed to abandon a man to the evil of his nature and then condemn him for what he could not avoid. On the falling righteous he asks whether a man once holy and pure can fall away so as to perish everlastingly and answers that he can, naming and rejecting the reading that makes it self-righteousness as the gloss of theologians, since God never speaks of turning away from what in his eyes is a nonentity and there is no holiness but what he infuses, so that a real righteous principle and practice is what is meant. Wesley takes the way for God's whole management of affairs and the charge to be that it does not square with his declared law.

debates.question: Is the denial that God has pleasure in the death of the wicked absolute or comparative?

positions.position: Comparative; God does take pleasure in these judgments as they fulfil his word and glorify his justice, but mercy is his delight and destruction his strange work.
Absolute, and it follows that he cannot have decreed to abandon a man to the evil of his nature and then condemn him for what he could not avoid.
A fundamental truth of both testaments, though it does not mean he can suffer his love to be set at nought.

debates.question: What righteousness does the falling righteous man lose?

positions.position: Not a true righteousness, which is Christ's imputed and cannot be lost, but a righteousness of his own esteem, ceremonial or at best merely moral.
A real righteous principle and practice; the self-righteousness reading is the gloss of theologians, since God never speaks of turning from what in his eyes is a nonentity.
A righteousness genuine but temporary, which never profits an apostate, since only perseverance is blessed.

outliers.claim: Finds the doctrine attested even outside the law and the prophets, since the heathen, though suffocated by errors, were moved by a secret impulse to seek pardon, as if the sense that God may be appeased by those who seek him were born with them.
Reads the word behind the complaint as literally weighed out or balanced, so the accusation is that God's dealing is unweighed and arbitrary rather than merely severe.

30.pericope_label: Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, saith the Lord God. Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin. Cast away from you all your transgressions, whereby ye have transgressed; and make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel? For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord God: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye.

schools.summary: Ellicott takes the last three verses as an earnest exhortation resting on the principles just declared, and denies that human sufficiency is in question anywhere in them: when the counsel is given to make a new heart and a new spirit it is not meant that this can ever be the work of any but God's Holy Spirit, yet that Spirit is given to those who ask, and the question of salvation remains one each man must decide for himself before God. The whole point of the chapter, on his reading, is that God's dealing with a man is determined by that man's own attitude toward him: whoever is alienated in heart, whatever his previous life, God will judge, and whoever now seeks to conform his life to God's will, God will receive and forgive.

Gill has the case fairly stated and the charge removed so that sentence may pass, and reads the casting away of the transgressions as the casting away of their idols, recording a Jewish commentator who took it instead of the punishment, which repentance might escape; on the final denial he again reads comparatively, taking the death for affliction, calamity and captivity, and the wish for their repenting and living on in their own land. Calvin hears authority in the judging clause, that they may plead as they please while God settles the strife in a word, since each is judged by his will and it is enough that the lawful judge pronounces them worthy of destruction whether they own it or not; he sees the objection coming that this exhortation puts conversion within free will, and answers that when God shows the elect a duty they know they cannot discharge they fly to the Spirit for help, so that the exhortation becomes the instrument by which the grace is conferred, resting the point on an old prayer that God would grant what he commands and command what he wishes; he separates the two words, the heart being the will and seat of the affections and the spirit the intellectual part, and concludes that since nothing less than a renewal of both would reconcile these people, nothing in us is sound and an entire renovation is needed.

Clarke asks for a holy violence that dashes away every incentive along with the act, and makes the asking do the work: call on God and he will give the new heart, and because you ask, he is pleased in some sort to attribute to you what his grace alone performs. He takes the closing question apart word by word, demanding one reason for the why, allowing nothing but obstinacy or a voluntary listlessness about salvation for the will, and reminding the ye that they are children of many mercies, fed all their life, redeemed, and pledged to renounce the pomps of the world. On the last denial he reads perdition, adds that no one is damned for having a fallen nature but only for refusing the grace that pardons it, and holds that since no man has more grace than will save himself, a parent's or relation's righteousness assists nobody. Wesley reduces the whole to a line: sinners displease God when they undo themselves, and please him when they return.

Henry frames the close as a verdict brought in on God's side after a fair trial at the bar of right reason, where judgment should follow and one would expect a sentence of condemnation, but a miracle of mercy intervenes and the day of grace is lengthened out, the whole ending in a call to repent with a promise of pardon attached. He counts four duties and finds an image for each: turn from sin and turn against it as an enemy you loathe, abandon it with a resolution never to return, give it a bill of divorce, break every league made with it, throw it overboard as the mariners threw the runaway prophet who raised the storm, and crucify it as a malefactor. On the new heart he says God does not command what cannot be done but bids us do what is in our power and pray for what is not; and on the closing question, that sinners die because they will die, going down the road to death and never coming up to the terms on which life is offered.

debates.question: How can men be commanded to make themselves a new heart if the new heart is God's gift?

positions.position: God does not command what cannot be done, but bids us do what is in our power and pray for what is not.
Call on God and he gives it; because we ask, he is pleased in some sort to attribute to us what his grace alone performs.
Human sufficiency is not in question; the new heart is the Spirit's work alone, but the Spirit is given to those who ask and the decision falls to each man.
The exhortation is itself the instrument by which the grace is conferred, since the elect, shown a duty they cannot discharge, fly to the Spirit for help.

debates.question: What death is denied to give God pleasure here?

positions.position: Affliction, calamity and captivity; the denial is comparative, and the wish is that they should repent and live on in their own land.
Perdition; no one is damned for a fallen nature, only for refusing the grace that pardons it.
Ruin of any kind, since sinners displease God when they undo themselves and please him when they return.

outliers.claim: Gives sin a bill of divorce and throws it overboard as the mariners threw the runaway prophet who had raised the storm, then crucifies it as a malefactor, stacking four images on one exhortation.
Distinguishes the heart as the will and seat of the affections from the spirit as the intellectual faculty, and argues that requiring both to be renewed shows nothing in us is sound.

themes: Therefore I will judge you, O house of Israel, every one according to his ways, saith the Lord God. Repent, and turn yourselves from all your transgressions; so iniquity shall not be your ruin.
Cast away from you all your transgressions, whereby ye have transgressed; and make you a new heart and a new spirit: for why will ye die, O house of Israel?
For I have no pleasure in the death of him that dieth, saith the Lord God: wherefore turn yourselves, and live ye.
